segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they were approaching Jerusalem, at Bethphage and Bethany near the Mount of Olives, he sent two of his disciples

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Go into the village ahead of you, and as soon as you enter it you will find a colt tied there, on which no one has ever sat. Untie it and bring it.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And if anyone says to you, ‘Why are you doing this?’ say, ‘The Lord needs it and will send it back here right away.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They went off and found a colt tied at a door, outside in the street, and they untied it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Some of those standing there said to them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “What are you doing, untying the colt?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They answered just as Jesus had told them, and the people let them go.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They brought the colt to Jesus and threw their cloaks over it, and he sat on it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Many people spread their cloaks on the road, and others spread leafy branches they had cut in the fields.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Those who went ahead and those who followed were shouting,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Hosanna! Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord!

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Blessed is the coming kingdom of our father David! Hosanna in the highest!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He entered Jerusalem and went into the temple. After looking around at everything, since the hour was already late, he went out to Bethany with the Twelve.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The next day, as they were leaving Bethany, he was hungry.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Seeing in the distance a fig tree in leaf, he went to see whether he might find anything on it. But when he came to it he found nothing but leaves, for it was not the season for figs.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In response he said to it,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “May no one ever eat fruit from you again.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And his disciples were listening.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They came to Jerusalem. Entering the temple, he began to drive out those who were selling and those who were buying in the temple, and he overturned the tables of the money changers and the seats of those selling doves,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and he would not allow anyone to carry anything through the temple.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He was teaching them and saying,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Is it not written, ‘My house will be called a house of prayer for all the nations’? But you have made it a den of bandits.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The chief priests and the scribes heard this and began looking for a way to destroy him; for they were afraid of him, because the whole crowd was astonished at his teaching.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When evening came, they went out of the city.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As they passed by in the morning, they saw the fig tree withered from the roots up.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Peter remembered and said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Rabbi, look! The fig tree you cursed has withered.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Have faith in God.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Truly I tell you, whoever says to this mountain, ‘Be lifted up and thrown into the sea,’ and does not doubt in their heart but believes that what they say will happen, it will be done for them.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For this reason I tell you, whatever you pray and ask for, believe that you have received it, and it will be yours.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And whenever you stand praying, if you have anything against anyone, forgive it, so that your Father in the heavens may also forgive you your offenses.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They came again to Jerusalem. As he was walking in the temple, the chief priests, the scribes and the elders came to him

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “By what authority are you doing these things? Or who gave you this authority to do them?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “I will ask you one question. Answer me, and I will tell you by what authority I am doing these things.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: John’s baptism—was it from heaven or from people? Answer me.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They argued it out among themselves, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “What should we say? If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will say, ‘Then why did you not believe him?’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: But should we say, ‘From people’?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They were afraid of the crowd, for everyone held that John really was a prophet.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So they answered Jesus,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “We do not know.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And Jesus said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Neither will I tell you by what authority I am doing these things.”

notes.traditional: The Lord has need of it
notes.note: The Greek word means “lord”, “master” or “owner”, and the phrase can also be construed as “its owner needs it”. Most translations take it as a reference to Jesus, as here, though whether bystanders would have heard a title or simply “the master” is uncertain. The promise to send the colt back is taken as part of the message the disciples are to give.

A Hebrew or Aramaic expression meaning “save, please”, taken from Psalm 118:25. The next line, “Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord”, is from Psalm 118:26, a psalm sung at the pilgrim festivals. By the first century the word seems to have become a shout of acclamation as well as a plea, and Mark leaves it untranslated.

notes.phrase: it was not the season for figs
notes.traditional: it was not the season for figs
notes.note: Passover falls in spring, well before the main fig harvest, though a tree in full leaf might carry small early figs. Mark splits the fig tree story around the temple incident, and most interpreters read the two together, with the fruitless tree as an acted sign about the temple. How far Mark intends that symbolism is debated.

The word covers the whole temple complex, not just the sanctuary building. The trading took place in the large outer court, the only area open to non-Jews. Money changers exchanged everyday coinage for the currency accepted for temple dues, and doves were sold as sacrificial offerings, especially for the poor.

The quotation is from Isaiah 56:7. The Greek word for “nations” is the same one this translation elsewhere renders “Gentiles”. In the plural it means the non-Jewish peoples, which gives the saying its point in the court to which they were admitted.

notes.traditional: a den of robbers (KJV: a den of thieves)
notes.note: The phrase echoes Jeremiah 7:11. The Greek word denotes a violent, often armed plunderer such as a highwayman or brigand, not a sneak thief or a cheating trader, and the “den” is the cave where such men hide out. Most modern translations have “robbers”; “bandits” is used here to keep the note of violence and outlawry and to match the same word at the arrest and crucifixion.

The Greek conjunction usually means “whenever”, and the verb is in a tense that can describe repeated action, so the sentence may mean “Whenever evening came, they would go out of the city”, describing the routine of the whole week. In the Greek of this period the same construction can also refer to a single occasion, which is how it is taken here. Translations and commentators are divided.

The Greek is literally “have faith of God”. Nearly all interpreters take God as the object of the faith, as here. A few have read it as “hold on to God’s faithfulness”, but the following verses about believing and not doubting favor the usual reading.

The Greek is plural, reflecting a Hebrew and Aramaic way of speaking that a first-century hearer would have recognized. Most translations flatten it to “heaven”. This translation keeps the plural where the Greek has it.

The word means a wrongful act against God or another person. “Trespasses” is the rendering of the Tyndale and King James tradition and of several modern versions, but in current English it mainly suggests entering property without permission. The meaning is not disputed, only the best English word, and “offense” is a standard lexicon gloss.

Many later manuscripts add a verse 26: “But if you do not forgive, neither will your Father in the heavens forgive your offenses.” It is absent from the earliest and best witnesses and is generally thought to have been added under the influence of Matthew 6:15. The Greek text translated here omits it, which is why the numbering passes from 25 to 27.

“Heaven” here is a reverent Jewish way of saying “God”. The question is whether John’s baptism was authorized by God or was a merely human undertaking. The answer bears directly on Jesus’ own authority, since John had pointed to him.

candidates.reason: “Scribe” suggests a copyist to modern readers, while the word denotes a trained expert in the Law; versions vary between “scribes”, “teachers of the law” and “legal experts”, and it recurs throughout the Gospels and Acts.

It denotes the whole temple complex as distinct from ναός, the sanctuary; a decision is needed on whether to distinguish the two in English (“temple courts” versus “temple”/“sanctuary”) across the Gospels, Acts and Paul.
It ranges across “authority”, “power”, “right” and “jurisdiction” and recurs in every part of the New Testament, so readers benefit from a controlled set of renderings by sense.
It is rendered variously “cloak”, “garment”, “coat”, “robe” and “clothes” across versions; the outer-garment sense needs one consistent English word, distinct from χιτών.

The middle/passive sense “doubt, waver” (also Matthew 21:21, Romans 4:20, 14:23, James 1:6) is debated against “dispute” or “be divided”, and needs one decision alongside the active sense “judge, distinguish”.
